domains.name: Natural Language Processing Engineering
domains.summary: The engineering track for machines that read and write: preprocessing decisions, subword tokenization and embeddings, classical NLTK methods as baselines, sequence models and decoding, and the Hugging Face practitioner workflow. Independent study; confers no certificate.

scenarios.title: The negation that vanished
scenarios.situation: A sentiment classifier on product reviews strips stopwords with a standard English list before featurizing. Accuracy is mediocre, and error analysis shows 'not good', 'never works', and 'no complaints' are systematically misclassified as positive or negative — the opposite of their meaning.
scenarios.prompt: What preprocessing change fixes this class of error?
choices: Stop stripping meaning-carrying words: keep negations ('not', 'never', 'no') and consider keeping stopwords entirely for short-text sentiment. Preprocessing must match the task — aggressive normalization that helps topic models destroys the signal sentiment depends on.
Lowercase more aggressively: case is the real noise here.
Remove even more stopwords: the list was too short.
Stem every token: 'working' and 'works' must merge.
scenarios.why: Stopword removal was designed for long-document retrieval, where frequent words add noise. In short reviews, 'not' is often the single most informative token in the sentence. The general rule: never apply a normalization step without checking what task-relevant signal it deletes.
scenarios.hint: Which single token flips the meaning of 'not good' — and is it on the stopword list you removed?

scenarios.title: The OOV explosion
scenarios.situation: A word-level tokenizer on social media text produces 30% out-of-vocabulary tokens at inference: misspellings, slang, emoji-adjacent glue words, and novel hashtags all map to UNK. The classifier trained on clean news text collapses on this data.
scenarios.prompt: What tokenization strategy addresses this robustly?
choices: Move to subword tokenization (BPE or WordPiece): frequent words stay whole while rare or misspelled words split into known pieces, so almost nothing is truly out-of-vocabulary and morphological variants share representations.
Grow the word vocabulary to 500k entries: a bigger lookup table fixes OOV.
Lowercase everything: case variants cause most OOVs.
Switch to pure character-level modeling: subwords are a fad.
scenarios.why: Word-level vocabularies have a hard coverage ceiling on noisy text; every unseen word becomes the same UNK vector. Subword methods learn the merge operations from data, so 'unhappiness' splits into pieces the model has seen even if the exact word is new. This is why modern pretrained models ship subword tokenizers.
scenarios.hint: What happens to a word the vocabulary has never seen — and what would you need for it to still get a useful representation?

scenarios.title: One vector for 'bank'
scenarios.situation: A team uses pretrained Word2Vec embeddings for a legal-document classifier. The word 'bank' gets one vector, so 'river bank erosion' and 'bank loan default' pull the document representation in the same direction. Precision on finance-vs-environment classification is stuck.
choices: Switch to contextual embeddings from a transformer encoder: the vector for 'bank' is computed from its surrounding words, so 'river bank' and 'bank loan' get different representations. Static embeddings assign one vector per word type; contextual models assign one per word occurrence.
Train Word2Vec with more dimensions: 300 is too few for polysemy.
Train Word2Vec longer: the vectors have not converged.
Average the word vectors with TF-IDF weights: weighting fixes polysemy.
scenarios.why: This is the distributional hypothesis hitting its limit: static embeddings conflate all senses of a word into one point. Contextual models (ELMo, BERT and descendants) made the representation a function of the sentence, which is why they ended the one-vector-per-word era for most tasks.
scenarios.hint: If a word has two unrelated meanings, can a single fixed vector represent both faithfully — and what information would you need to disambiguate them?

scenarios.title: The looping chatbot
scenarios.situation: A seq2seq support chatbot trained on dialog pairs answers fluently but, on open-ended prompts, falls into loops: 'I don't know I don't know I don't know...' Greedy decoding picks the highest-probability token at each step.
scenarios.prompt: What decoding change breaks the loop?
choices: Replace pure greedy decoding with beam search or sampling (temperature/top-k/top-p) plus a repetition penalty or no-repeat n-gram constraint. Greedy decoding is myopic — one safe, high-probability token ('I') leads into a self-reinforcing loop the model cannot back out of.
Train on more data: the model has not seen enough dialogs.
Use a bigger model: capacity fixes decoding loops.
Lower the learning rate and retrain: optimization is the issue.
scenarios.why: The loop is a decoding artifact, not a knowledge gap: 'I don't know' is high-probability under the training distribution, and greedy selection keeps re-selecting it because each repeated token raises the next one's probability. Sampling introduces diversity; repetition penalties directly tax already-used n-grams.
scenarios.hint: Once the model emits 'I don't know' twice, why would a greedy decoder pick it a third time — and what would let it choose differently?

scenarios.title: The confident pipeline
scenarios.situation: A team ships a sentiment feature using a Hugging Face pipeline with a general-domain checkpoint. On their legal-contract text it returns confident labels that domain experts say are wrong — the model was trained on movie reviews and tweets, not contracts.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct engineering response?
choices: Treat the pipeline as a baseline, not a solution: there is domain shift. Read the model card to confirm the training domain, collect labeled in-domain data, and fine-tune (or train a domain-specific classifier). Do not trust confidence scores from a model operating outside its training distribution.
Trust the confidence scores: 0.97 means it is right.
Rephrase the inputs as prompts: the pipeline just needs better phrasing.
Ensemble two pipelines: averaging fixes domain shift.
scenarios.why: Confidence is not correctness — softmax scores are poorly calibrated under distribution shift, and the model card exists precisely to tell you what domain the checkpoint was trained on. The pipeline API is the fastest way to get a baseline; fine-tuning on your data is how you get a product.
scenarios.hint: What data was this checkpoint actually trained on — and how would you check before trusting it on contracts?

scenarios.title: The fine-tune that forgot
scenarios.situation: Fine-tuning a BERT-base classifier on 400 labeled support tickets with lr=1e-3 for 20 epochs: training accuracy hits 100% by epoch 3, validation F1 collapses, and the model now performs worse than the pretrained baseline on a related task — it forgot general language structure.
choices: Fine-tune gently: learning rate around 2e-5 with warmup, 2-4 epochs, small batches, and early stopping on validation — optionally freezing lower layers first. With 400 examples the pretrained weights are the asset; a large LR and long schedule destroy them (catastrophic forgetting) while memorizing the tiny set.
Train for 50 epochs: more training always helps small datasets.
Raise the learning rate to 1e-2: the model needs bigger steps to learn the new task.
Switch to a larger model: BERT-large memorizes small data better.
scenarios.why: Pretrained models need only small nudges: the standard recipe (low LR, few epochs, warmup) exists because aggressive fine-tuning overwrites the general representations that made the checkpoint valuable. With 400 examples you are adapting, not training — and early stopping on a validation split is non-negotiable.
scenarios.hint: You have 400 examples and 110M parameters — which side of that ratio should dominate the training schedule, and what does that imply for the learning rate?

scenarios.title: The OOV explosion
scenarios.situation: Production sees 25% OOV on new slang.
choices: Subword tokenizers + periodic vocab refresh + monitoring — OOV is operational
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. OOV is an operational concern: subword fallback, monitored rates, scheduled vocab refreshes.

scenarios.title: The bank problem
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Polysemy needs contextual representations — static vectors conflate senses.

domains.name: Systems Anatomy: Seeing Systems as Living Flows
domains.description: Learn to see Nlp Engineering as living systems — not static diagrams, but moving sequences where every part connects. Master systems thinking for exams and interviews.

scenarios.title: The Natural Language Processing Engineering Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that Natural Language Processing Engineering is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Natural Language Processing Engineering?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Natural Language Processing Engineering issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Natural Language Processing Engineering is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is Natural Language Processing Engineering supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any Natural Language Processing Engineering failure in Nlp Engineering.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
objectives: Apply systems anatomy to Natural Language Processing Engineering
evidence: All Natural Language Processing Engineering components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

domains.name: Text Preprocessing
domains.description: Cleaning, normalizing, and preparing text for models.

scenarios.title: The negation that vanished
choices: Handle negation: bigrams/negation scope features or contextual models — 'not' flips polarity
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Negation scope is the classic sentiment trap: unigram models see 'good' and miss 'not'. Bigrams, negation tagging, or contextual models fix it.

scenarios.title: The OOV explosion
choices: Subword tokenization (BPE/WordPiece) — OOV becomes composable pieces
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Subword tokenizers decompose unknowns into known pieces — the standard OOV solution.

scenarios.title: The encoding mess
choices: Fix encoding: decode as the correct charset (UTF-8), normalize unicode (NFKC)
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Mojibake = wrong charset decoding; fix the decode chain and normalize unicode forms.

scenarios.title: The dup leak
choices: Train/test duplicates — near-dup removal before splitting
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Duplicates across splits leak test into train — dedupe BEFORE splitting, always.

scenarios.title: The Mr. problem
scenarios.situation: Sentence splitter breaks on 'Mr. Smith went...'.
choices: Abbreviation-aware segmentation — exception lists or trained sentencizers
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Naive period-splitting breaks on abbreviations; use exception-aware or statistical sentencizers.

scenarios.title: The emoji signal
scenarios.situation: Stripping emojis drops sentiment accuracy 8 points.
choices: Emojis carry signal — profile before stripping; keep what's predictive
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Preprocessing must be evidence-driven: profile, ablate, keep what helps. Emojis are sentiment features.

scenarios.title: The pipeline skew
scenarios.situation: Training used v1 cleaning; serving uses v2.
choices: Train/serve skew — identical preprocessing code and versions both sides
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Any preprocessing difference between train and serve is skew — version and share the exact pipeline.

domains.name: Embeddings
domains.description: Word vectors to sentence transformers: representing meaning.

scenarios.title: One vector for 'bank'
choices: Static embeddings conflate senses — need contextual (per-occurrence) vectors
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. One vector per word-type cannot represent multiple senses — contextual embeddings (BERT-style) produce per-occurrence vectors.

scenarios.title: The retrieval pick
choices: Sentence transformer — trained for semantic similarity
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Sentence transformers are trained explicitly for semantic similarity — the retrieval workhorse.

scenarios.title: The hard negatives
choices: Hard negatives — easy negatives teach nothing; mine top-k confusions
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Contrastive learning needs informative negatives — mined hard negatives drive the gains.

scenarios.title: The padding bug
scenarios.situation: Sentence embeddings degrade on short texts.
choices: Attention mask in pooling — unmasked padding pollutes the mean
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Mean-pooling without masking averages in padding vectors — always mask.

scenarios.title: The domain gap
scenarios.situation: Generic embeddings fail on medical queries.
choices: Domain fine-tune with contrastive loss on medical pairs
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Domain shift demands domain tuning — fine-tune on in-domain pairs with hard negatives.

scenarios.title: The index choice
choices: Managed vector DB (Pinecone/Qdrant cloud) with HNSW — ops offloaded
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Scale + latency SLO + managed ops → managed vector DB with HNSW indexing.

scenarios.title: The hybrid win
choices: Hybrid dense + BM25 — keywords catch exact codes
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Exact codes need keyword matching — hybrid fusion is the robust default.

domains.name: Sequence Models
domains.description: RNNs, LSTMs, and when they still matter.

scenarios.title: The long dependency
choices: LSTM/GRU or transformer — vanilla RNN gradients vanish
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. 200 steps exceeds vanilla RNN memory; gated or attention architectures handle long dependencies.

scenarios.title: The tiny device
choices: Small LSTM/GRU or distilled model — microseconds on CPU, tiny memory
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Microcontroller budgets demand tiny gated models — transformers don't fit.

scenarios.title: The NER baseline
choices: BiLSTM-CRF or small transformer — strong baselines before scaling
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. 5k sentences supports strong baselines; climb the ladder from there with measurements.

scenarios.title: The invalid tags
choices: CRF layer — models label dependencies, forbids invalid transitions
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Independent per-token softmax can't enforce BIO constraints; CRFs decode globally valid sequences.

scenarios.title: The streaming need
choices: Unidirectional RNN/LSTM or cached transformer — streaming-native
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Streaming forbids future context — unidirectional recurrence or KV-cached generation.

scenarios.title: The lineage question
choices: Parallel training + long dependencies via attention — solved RNN bottlenecks
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Attention removed sequential bottlenecks (parallelism) and vanishing gradients (direct access) — architectural, not hype.

scenarios.title: The ladder
choices: Baseline first (logreg/LSTM), then small transformer — climb the ladder
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Baselines calibrate expectations and often suffice; escalate with measurements.

domains.name: Transformer Engineering
domains.description: Building with transformers: HuggingFace, training, debugging.

scenarios.title: The LoRA pick
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. QLoRA is THE single-GPU fine-tuning standard: quantized frozen base, trainable low-rank adapters.

scenarios.title: The NaN loss
choices: Lower LR, enable clipping, check bf16 — then resume from checkpoint
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. NaN = instability: LR, precision, or bad batch. Systematic fixes, then resume — checkpoints exist for this.

scenarios.title: The tiny test
scenarios.situation: New training setup — verify it works.
choices: Overfit a tiny subset — if it can't memorize 10 examples, something's broken
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The tiny-subset overfit test is the fastest bug detector in deep learning.

scenarios.title: The eval gap
choices: Evaluate on YOUR task — benchmark scores don't transfer
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Benchmarks measure benchmarks; your task needs your eval.

scenarios.title: The Hub leverage
choices: Fine-tune a Hub pretrained model — transfer beats scratch 99% of the time
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Pretrained transfer dominates from-scratch training for nearly all practical tasks.

scenarios.title: The pipeline trap
choices: Inflexible: no batching control, error handling, or optimization — write custom serving
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Pipelines are for prototyping; production needs custom batching, validation, and monitoring.

scenarios.title: The seed story
choices: Set and log all seeds (Python/NumPy/Torch/CUDA) — stochasticity controlled
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Unseeded runs are anecdotes; seed everything and report variance honestly.

scenarios.title: The 2am failure
choices: Orchestration with retries + alerts + stage metrics — monitored, not cron
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Orchestrators (Airflow/Prefect) retry, alert, and expose per-stage health — cron fails silently.

scenarios.title: The rerun corruption
choices: Non-idempotent stages — reruns must be safe; design for it
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Idempotency is a design requirement: same input, same output, safe reruns.

scenarios.title: The boundary bug
scenarios.situation: Stage 3 gets malformed input from stage 2.
choices: Schema contracts + validation at stage boundaries
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Validate at boundaries with schemas (Great Expectations) — catch corruption where it crosses.

scenarios.title: The batch bill
choices: Spot instances + right-sizing + checkpointing — batch economics
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Batch is elastic: spot pricing, right-sized workers, checkpointed progress.

scenarios.title: The streaming question
scenarios.situation: Daily report pipeline — batch or stream?
choices: Batch — daily latency needs don't justify streaming ops cost
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Streaming's operational cost needs a latency justification; daily reports don't have one.

scenarios.title: The golden docs
choices: Golden documents: fixed inputs with expected outputs, run in CI
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Golden-document E2E tests in CI catch regressions before 2am does.

scenarios.title: The slow stage
choices: Profile per-stage metrics — find and parallelize the bottleneck
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Per-stage observability reveals the bottleneck; parallelize the embarrassingly parallel parts.

scenarios.title: The κ=0.4
choices: Rewrite guidelines: pilot, adjudicate, clarify edge cases
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Low κ indicts the task design — iterate guidelines with adjudicated examples.

scenarios.title: The budget
choices: Active learning — label the most informative 10k via uncertainty sampling
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Active learning routinely achieves 5-10x label efficiency — the budget-stretching standard.

scenarios.title: The gold set
choices: Gold validation set — human-labeled truth to anchor evaluation
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Weak supervision needs gold anchors — otherwise you can't measure true quality.

scenarios.title: The edge cases
choices: Explicit edge-case rules in guidelines with examples
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Edge cases need written resolutions — without them, annotators roulette.

scenarios.title: The drift
choices: Guideline rot or harder data — re-pilot, refresh training, check the stream
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Agreement drift signals stale guidelines or shifting data — diagnose, don't punish.

scenarios.title: The tool pick
choices: Use Label Studio/Prodigy — labeling tools are solved problems
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Don't build labeling infrastructure — mature open tools exist.

scenarios.title: The expert task
scenarios.situation: Complex legal NER via crowd workers.
choices: Skill mismatch — experts for hard tasks; crowds for simple
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Match workforce skill to task difficulty — legal NER needs domain experts.

scenarios.title: The two stages
choices: Two-stage: fast retrieval (candidates) then precise reranking
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Scale demands staging: cheap recall first, expensive precision on top-k.

scenarios.title: The metric pick
choices: NDCG@10 — graded relevance with position discount
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Ranking needs ranking metrics: NDCG handles graded relevance and position.

scenarios.title: The known-item
choices: MRR — reciprocal rank of the first relevant result
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Known-item search cares about the FIRST hit's rank — MRR's design center.

scenarios.title: The query fail
choices: Spell correction + synonyms in query understanding
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Query normalization (spelling, synonyms, entities) fixes most 'no results' cases.

scenarios.title: The latency budget
choices: Distill/smaller reranker, fewer candidates, or cascade — meet the budget
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Latency budgets are constraints: smaller models, fewer candidates, cascading — engineer to the SLO.

scenarios.title: The feedback loop
choices: Feedback loops — optimize long-term satisfaction, add guardrails
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Online metrics need guardrails: clickbait wins CTR while destroying trust — measure satisfaction too.

scenarios.title: The hybrid retrieval
scenarios.situation: Dense misses SKUs, BM25 misses synonyms.
choices: Hybrid — fuse both; each covers the other's weakness
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Hybrid retrieval is the robust default: keywords for exact, dense for semantic.

domains.name: Conversational AI
domains.description: Dialogue systems: design, state, and guardrails.

scenarios.title: The loop
scenarios.situation: Bot and user repeat the same clarification 4 times.
choices: Repair strategy + handoff trigger — detect loops, escalate gracefully
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Loop detection → repair attempt → human handoff is the dialogue design pattern for stuck conversations.

scenarios.title: The injection
choices: Input guardrails: instruction hierarchy, untrusted-input handling
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Guardrail layers treat user input as untrusted — instruction hierarchy plus filters.

scenarios.title: The amnesia
scenarios.situation: Bot forgets the user's name mid-conversation.
choices: Explicit dialogue state: slots + summary persisted per turn
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Structured state tracking (slots, summaries) beats hoping the context window suffices.

scenarios.title: The metric
choices: Task success rate + turns-to-success + human eval — not fluency alone
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Dialogue quality = goal achievement efficiency, measured properly.

scenarios.title: The handoff
scenarios.situation: Angry user stuck with bot for 10 minutes.
choices: No handoff triggers — frustration + low confidence should escalate with context
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Missing escalation design traps users; warm handoffs with summaries preserve trust.

scenarios.title: The stakes
choices: Human-in-loop + disclaimers + guardrails — high-stakes needs oversight
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. High-stakes domains demand human oversight, uncertainty communication, and strict guardrails.

scenarios.title: The personality
scenarios.situation: Bot's tone swings wildly between turns.
choices: System prompt personality spec + consistency eval
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Consistent voice needs an explicit spec, tested — personality is a product requirement.

scenarios.title: The pattern pick
choices: Online streaming via vLLM — token-by-token UX within budget
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Interactive chat needs online streaming inference — batch is a UX disaster here.

scenarios.title: The throughput
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. 5% utilization screams no-batching — continuous batching is the standard fix.

scenarios.title: The stale cache
scenarios.situation: Cache serves outputs from model v1 after v2 deploy.
choices: Cache key missing model version — include it always
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Model version belongs in every cache key — otherwise deploys serve stale outputs.

scenarios.title: The contract
scenarios.situation: Clients break on every model update.
choices: Versioned API (/v1/) with typed schemas — contracts endure
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Versioned, typed contracts let models evolve without breaking clients.

scenarios.title: The GPU waste
choices: Right-size: single smaller GPU or shared serving — match hardware to load
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Hardware must match load — 3% utilization on 8×A100 is money fire.

scenarios.title: The retry storm
choices: Idempotency keys — safe retries by design
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Idempotency keys make retries safe — essential API hygiene.

scenarios.title: The unit economics
scenarios.situation: CFO asks serving cost per 1k inferences.
choices: Measured $/1k by model version — tracked, with cost levers listed
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Unit economics per model version is the serving cost discipline — measure it.

scenarios.title: The untracked best
scenarios.situation: Best model came from an untracked run.
choices: Track everything from run one — untracked wins are irreproducible
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Experiment tracking is non-negotiable — the best untracked model is a loss.

scenarios.title: The silent decay
scenarios.situation: Model accuracy drifted 15 points over 6 months.
choices: Drift monitoring + retraining playbook — detect and respond
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Language drifts; production NLP needs drift detection and a retraining playbook — not one-time training.

scenarios.title: The deploy
scenarios.situation: New model version — how to ship safely?
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Canary rollouts with automatic rollback on metric regression is the safe deployment pattern.

scenarios.title: The zombie
scenarios.situation: Three old model versions still serving traffic.
choices: Model registry with lifecycle: stage, deprecate, retire — no zombies
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Version lifecycle management retires old models cleanly — zombies are a governance failure.

scenarios.title: The card
choices: Model card: intended use, evals, limitations, data — ready before asked
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Model cards prepared proactively make audits routine instead of scrambles.

scenarios.title: The smoke test
scenarios.situation: Broken code merged; training wasted a day.
choices: CI smoke training on every PR — catch breaks before they cost GPU-days
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Small smoke-training in CI catches breakage before expensive runs.

scenarios.title: The feedback
scenarios.situation: Users report bad outputs; team unaware.
choices: Feedback loop + monitoring — user signals must reach the team
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Production feedback loops (reports → triage → fix) close the quality cycle.

scenarios.title: The negation blindspot
choices: Behavioral CheckList tests — capability-targeted, not just accuracy
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. CheckList-style behavioral tests probe capabilities (negation, NER) that aggregate accuracy hides.

scenarios.title: The flaky test
scenarios.situation: Tests call the live API; CI fails randomly.
choices: Mock model calls in unit tests — deterministic fixtures
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Unit tests must be deterministic — mock external model calls; test integration separately.

scenarios.title: The silent regression
scenarios.situation: New version worse on old cases; nobody noticed.
choices: Golden-set regression gates on every release
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Golden sets with diff review gate every release — regressions become visible before users see them.

scenarios.title: The typo attack
choices: Adversarial typo tests → training augmentation or normalization
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Test adversarially, then fix via augmentation or input normalization — robustness is engineered.

scenarios.title: The 2am OOM
choices: Load test to 10x before launch — find limits early
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Load testing reveals breaking points before users do — capacity planning from measurements.

scenarios.title: The round-trip
choices: Property test on the invariant — round-trips must hold
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Property-based tests encode invariants (round-trips, idempotency) that catch subtle bugs.

scenarios.title: The soak leak
scenarios.situation: Memory grows over 4 hours under load.
choices: Soak testing — sustained load reveals leaks drift misses
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Soak tests (hours of sustained load) surface leaks and drift that short tests miss.

lessons.title: Natural Language Processing Engineering — Core concepts
concepts: Preprocessing is task-dependent: normalization that helps topic modeling (stopword removal, stemming) can destroy sentiment signal ('not good'). Never apply a text transform without asking what it deletes.

Tokenization is the representation contract: word-level vocabularies drown in OOV on noisy text, while BPE/WordPiece subwords split rare words into known pieces — the reason modern models ship subword tokenizers.

Embeddings encode the distributional hypothesis — words appearing in similar contexts get similar vectors. Word2Vec and GloVe made this practical; static embeddings assign one vector per word type, conflating all senses.

Classical NLTK tools (tokenizers, POS taggers, chunkers, named-entity chunkers) are fast, inspectable baselines: still the right choice for small, well-defined tasks and for features that neural models should not have to relearn.

Sequence models made language modeling the unifying task: RNNs and LSTMs carry state across tokens, seq2seq with attention maps sequences to sequences, and decoding strategy (greedy, beam, sampling) shapes output as much as the model does.

The Hugging Face workflow is pipeline first, fine-tune second: instant baselines from the pipelines API, then task-specific fine-tuning on your data — after reading the model card for training domain, license, and known limits.

example.code:
from transformers import pipeline, AutoTokenizer

# Baseline in two lines: tokenizer + model + labels, handled for you.
clf = pipeline("sentiment-analysis")
print(clf("The battery life is fantastic, but the screen is dim."))
# [{'label': 'POSITIVE', 'score': 0.99...}]

# Look under the hood before trusting it: what does the tokenizer see?
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(clf.model.name_or_path)
print(tok.tokenize("unhappiness"))
# ['un', '##happiness']  -> subwords, not UNK

# Fine-tuning (sketch): same tokenizer, new head, your labeled data.
# from transformers import AutoModelForSequenceClassification, Trainer
# model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(
#     "distilbert-base-uncased", num_labels=3)
# train with Trainer on your Dataset of tokenized examples,
# lr=2e-5, 3 epochs, early stopping on validation F1.
example.walkthrough: The pipelines API is the fastest honest baseline in NLP: it wires a pretrained tokenizer and model together and returns labeled predictions in two lines. Inspecting the tokenizer shows why subwords matter — 'unhappiness' splits into known pieces instead of collapsing to unknown. The fine-tuning sketch shows the production path: keep the pretrained tokenizer, attach a classification head, and train gently (low learning rate, few epochs) on your own labeled data. Between the two lines and the sketch sits the model card — read it before either, because the training domain decides whether the baseline is even valid.

pitfalls: Common trap: stripping stopwords for sentiment or short-text tasks — 'not', 'never', and 'no' are often the most informative tokens.
Common trap: trusting pipeline confidence scores on out-of-domain text — softmax confidence is not correctness under distribution shift.
Common trap: fine-tuning with a large learning rate or many epochs on a small dataset — you destroy the pretrained weights you came for.
Common trap: evaluating tokenization choices on intrinsic metrics instead of the downstream task — the tokenizer serves the task, not the other way around.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: From Static Diagrams to Living Systems
concepts: A textbook diagram shows you one part in isolation — a living systems view shows you how all parts of Nlp Engineering move together in sequence
The four-step systems anatomy method: (1) See the whole in context, (2) Cut it open to reveal layers, (3) Walk through the process step-by-step, (4) Pull apart into labeled pieces
Apply this to any system in this course: start with the trigger action, trace through every component it touches, watch the data flow
Interview/exam power: when asked 'how does X work?', narrate the journey — 'it starts here, then...'. This demonstrates senior-level systems thinking

example.code:
TRIGGER event occurs
  → First system receives it (see the handoff)
  → Processing happens in sequence (watch each step)
  → State changes propagate (follow the ripple)
  → Final outcome delivered

Each arrow is a living handoff, not a static box.
example.walkthrough: This is the 'jet engine cutaway' for your field: instead of memorizing isolated facts, you see the entire flow as a moving sequence. Practice narrating this journey out loud.

pitfalls: Memorizing terms without understanding the processes they participate in
Drawing architecture diagrams as boxes without showing the data flow between them
Answering 'how does X work?' with a definition instead of walking through the sequence
lessons.try_it: Pick any process in this course. Write out the full journey from trigger to outcome, naming every system touched.

lessons.title: Anatomy of Natural Language Processing Engineering
concepts: Natural Language Processing Engineering is a multi-step process within Natural Language Processing Engineering: trace the full sequence from initiation to completion
See it as a journey: identify the trigger, follow each handoff, watch state change at every step
Every step depends on the previous — a failure at any point breaks the chain. Map these dependencies
Connect Natural Language Processing Engineering to the broader Natural Language Processing Engineering ecosystem — nothing operates in isolation

example.code:
Step 1: Initiation
  Natural Language Processing Engineering begins — what triggers it?

Step 2: Processing
  Data flows through — what transforms it?

Step 3: Handoff
  Result passes to next system — what is the interface?

Step 4: Completion
  Final state reached — how do you verify?
example.walkthrough: Apply the four-step anatomy method to Natural Language Processing Engineering. Draw it as a flowing sequence, not a static diagram.

pitfalls: Treating Natural Language Processing Engineering as an isolated component instead of part of a living flow
Skipping the dependency mapping — not asking 'what does this step need from the previous?'
Memorizing the steps without understanding WHY each one exists
lessons.try_it: Whiteboard the full Natural Language Processing Engineering flow from memory. Label every handoff and dependency.

lessons.title: How to Use This Bootcamp: Natural Language Processing Engineering
concepts: This bootcamp is organized as a guided path: Start Here → domains in order → scenarios → labs → mock assessment. Follow the sequence; each domain unlocks the next at 80% completion.
Lessons teach concepts with worked examples. Scenarios test application under realistic conditions. Labs give hands-on reps. The mock assessment simulates the real thing under time pressure.

The study order is deliberate: Start Here → text-preprocessing → embeddings → sequence-models → transformer-engineering → nlp-pipelines → data-labeling → search-ranking → conversational-ai → model-serving → mlops-nlp → nlp-testing → systems-anatomy → capstone → mock
Track your progress on the dashboard. Revisit weak domains — spaced repetition beats cramming. Aim for mastery (correct streaks), not just completion.

example.code:
STUDY LOOP (repeat per domain):
  1. Read the lessons — take notes in your own words
  2. Run the scenarios — explain your reasoning before submitting
  3. Do the labs — hands-on reps lock in muscle memory
  4. Check the dashboard — below 80%? Loop again before moving on
example.walkthrough: Work one domain at a time. From raw text to production NLP: preprocessing, embeddings, pipelines, serving, and MLOps. Finish every domain, then take the mock assessment under timed conditions.

pitfalls: Skipping ahead to the mock before finishing domains — the mock measures readiness, it does not build it.
Reading passively without doing scenarios and labs — recognition is not recall.
Ignoring the dashboard — weak domains compound; fix them early.
lessons.try_it: Right now: set up a Python NLP environment (spaCy + transformers + datasets) — you will use it every week.

lessons.title: Study Strategy: How to Master This Material
concepts: Active recall beats re-reading: after each lesson, close the page and explain the key ideas aloud in your own words.
Interleaving beats blocking: mix scenarios from different domains in one session to build discrimination skill.
Spaced repetition beats cramming: revisit completed domains after 1 day, 3 days, and 7 days.
Teach-back is the mastery test: if you can whiteboard a concept for a colleague, you own it.

example.code:
WEEKLY CADENCE:
  Mon–Fri: 1 domain per day (lessons + scenarios + labs)
  Saturday: mixed scenario review across all completed domains
  Sunday: rest or light flashcard review
  Repeat until dashboard shows 80%+ everywhere, then mock.
example.walkthrough: Consistency compounds. Ninety focused minutes daily beats a ten-hour weekend binge — your brain consolidates during sleep, so daily touchpoints win.

pitfalls: Cramming the night before — short-term memory evaporates under pressure.
Only doing what is comfortable — growth lives in the scenarios you get wrong.
No notes — writing forces encoding; highlight-only reading does not.
lessons.try_it: Right now: create a study log (paper or digital). After each session write 3 things learned and 1 thing still fuzzy.

lessons.title: Course Map: What You Will Learn
concepts: This bootcamp covers the full scope of Natural Language Processing Engineering, from foundations to advanced application.

Skipping systems-anatomy — it teaches the thinking skill that makes every other domain easier.

concepts: Scenarios are the core assessment: realistic situations with four options, hints, evidence panels, and detailed explanations.
Knowledge checks verify lesson comprehension — answer correctly and the lesson auto-completes. No empty clicking.
Labs are hands-on: follow the steps, run the commands, verify the outcome. Muscle memory matters.

SCORING MENTAL MODEL:

  Scenario correct, hint used → understood with support; revisit

example.walkthrough: Use every wrong answer as a diagnostic. The explanation tells you exactly which concept to revisit — follow that thread immediately.

pitfalls: Rushing scenarios to inflate completion — the dashboard measures streaks, not clicks.
Ignoring hints when stuck — a hint used and understood beats a guess.
Skipping the mock — timed practice is the only honest readiness signal.

lessons.title: Capstone Overview: Capstone: Ship an NLP System
concepts: Your capstone is a real, demonstrable project: Build and deploy a production NLP system with evals, monitoring, and documentation.
Pick one project and scope it to 2–4 weeks of part-time work. Smaller and finished beats ambitious and abandoned.
Document as you build: architecture decisions, problems hit, how you solved them. This becomes your interview story.
Publish the result: code repository, write-up, demo video. Employers and examiners trust artifacts over claims.

example.code:
PROJECT OPTIONS:
  1. Production text classifier — Train, serve via API, monitor drift; full MLOps loop
  2. Semantic search engine — Embeddings + vector DB + eval harness; deployed demo
  3. Support chatbot — RAG + guardrails + human handoff; measured resolution rate
  4. Multilingual pipeline — Preprocessing + model + eval across 3 languages
example.walkthrough: Choose your project by the end of this week. Write a one-page plan: goal, milestones, tech, done-criteria. Build and deploy a production NLP system with evals, monitoring, and documentation.

pitfalls: Choosing three projects — finish one brilliantly before starting a second.
Building without documenting — the write-up is half the value.
Tutorial-copying — extend it, break it, make it yours.
lessons.try_it: Right now: rank the project options above. Write two sentences on why your top pick fits your goals.

lessons.title: Build in Public: Documentation That Proves Skill
concepts: A README that explains the problem, your approach, and the result is worth more than the code alone.
Architecture diagrams show systems thinking. Decision logs show judgment. Test results show rigor.
Demo videos (2–5 min) let reviewers see it working without installing anything.
Link everything: resume → portfolio → repository → live demo. One click from claim to proof.

example.code:
README SKELETON:
  # Project name — one-line outcome
  ## Problem — who hurts and how
  ## Approach — architecture + key decisions
  ## Results — metrics, screenshots, demo link
  ## What I'd do next — shows growth mindset
example.walkthrough: Start your README on day one, not at the end. Fill it in as you build — it becomes your lab notebook.

pitfalls: README as afterthought — stale docs signal sloppy engineering.
No demo — 'trust me, it works' convinces nobody.
Hiding failures — 'what broke and how I fixed it' is the most credible section.
lessons.try_it: Create the repository and README skeleton today, even before writing code.

lessons.title: Presenting Your Capstone: The Interview Story
concepts: Structure your story: situation → complication → your action → result. Sixty seconds, crisp.
Lead with the outcome ('cut report time from 2 days to 20 minutes'), then explain how.
Prepare for deep follow-ups: 'why this approach over X?' — your decision log has the answers.
Connect the project to the role: map each project skill to a line in the job description.

example.code:
STORY TEMPLATE:
  'We had [problem] costing [impact]. I built [solution] using [tech].
   The hard part was [complication]; I solved it by [approach].
   Result: [metric]. Next I'd [improvement].'
example.walkthrough: Rehearse the story aloud three times. Record yourself once — painful but effective.

pitfalls: Rambling — practice the 60-second version until it is tight.
Only happy path — interviewers probe failures; own yours with the fix.
No metrics — 'it works' is weak; 'cut time 90%' is proof.
lessons.try_it: Write your 60-second capstone story now. Time yourself reading it aloud.

lessons.title: Cleaning and Normalization
concepts: Cleaning: strip HTML, fix encoding (UTF-8), normalize whitespace — the unglamorous 80%.
Normalization: lowercase (when case doesn't matter), unicode normalize (NFKC), expand contractions.
Deduplication: exact + near-dup removal — duplicates bias training and eval.
Language detection first: route to the right pipeline before processing.

example.code:
CLEANING PIPELINE:
  detect lang → fix encoding → strip markup
  → normalize unicode/whitespace → dedupe
example.walkthrough: Log what you remove — preprocessing decisions are experiment variables.

pitfalls: Aggressive cleaning — removing signal (e.g., casing in NER).
No dedup — train/test leakage via duplicates.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Clean 1000 raw documents; log every transformation applied.

lessons.title: Tokenization in Practice
concepts: Word tokenization: split on whitespace/punctuation — simple, language-dependent.
Subword (BPE/WordPiece): handles OOV via pieces — the modern default.
Sentence segmentation: needed for per-sentence tasks — abbreviations are the classic trap.
Choose per task: subword for transformers; words for classic ML baselines.

example.code:
TOKENIZER CHOICE:
  Transformer model? → its native subword tokenizer
  Classic ML? → word tokens + n-grams
  Always: same tokenizer train AND inference
example.walkthrough: Tokenizer mismatch between train and serve is a silent killer.

pitfalls: Mixed tokenizers — train/serve skew.
Ignoring sentence segmentation — 'Mr. Smith' splits wrong.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Tokenize 100 sentences two ways; compare OOV rates.

lessons.title: Linguistic Features: POS, NER, Parsing
concepts: POS tagging: grammatical roles — features for classic pipelines.
NER: persons, orgs, locations — spaCy/Stanza out of the box.
Dependency parsing: grammatical structure — relation extraction input.
Modern note: transformers often learn these implicitly — use explicit features when data is scarce.

example.code:
FEATURE LADDER:
  Enough data + transformer? → let it learn
  Small data? → explicit linguistic features help
example.walkthrough: spaCy pipelines give all three in one pass — start there.

pitfalls: Feature-stuffing — more features ≠ better; ablate.
Ignoring the transformer alternative — test both.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Run spaCy over 50 sentences; inspect POS/NER/parse outputs.

lessons.title: Handling Messy Real-World Text
concepts: Social text: emojis, slang, typos — normalize or embrace (domain models).
OCR output: character errors — fuzzy matching and robust tokenizers.
Code-switching: mixed languages — detect per-segment or use multilingual models.
Rule: profile your data FIRST (length, language, noise) — then design.

example.code:
DATA PROFILE:
  □ Length distribution □ Language mix
  □ Noise types □ Duplicates
  → then design preprocessing
example.walkthrough: An hour of profiling saves days of debugging.

pitfalls: Assuming clean data — profile first, always.
One pipeline for all noise — match to the profile.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Profile a messy dataset; write the 1-page data report.

lessons.title: Preprocessing as Code: Reproducible Pipelines
concepts: Version your preprocessing — same code, same data, same output, every time.
Separate: raw → cleaned → tokenized stages with checksums at each.
Test: unit tests on edge cases (empty, emoji-only, 10k chars).
Document decisions: WHY each step exists — future you will forget.

example.code:
PIPELINE CONTRACT:
  raw/ (immutable) → clean/ (script v1.2)
  → tokens/ (script v1.2) + manifest.json
example.walkthrough: Preprocessing is part of the model — version it like one.

pitfalls: In-place mutation — raw data must be immutable.
Undocumented steps — irreproducible.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Write preprocessing with a manifest; re-run and diff outputs.

lessons.title: Word Embeddings: Word2Vec, GloVe, FastText
concepts: Distributional hypothesis: words in similar contexts have similar vectors.
Word2Vec (skip-gram/CBOW), GloVe (co-occurrence), FastText (subword — handles OOV/morphology).
Analogies (king - man + woman ≈ queen) show linear structure — but don't overclaim.
Static embeddings: one vector per word — 'bank' gets one meaning (the limitation).

example.code:
WHEN STATIC SUFFICES:
  Baseline features, constrained compute
  → FastText (subword-aware, fast)
example.walkthrough: Static embeddings are baselines now — know them, then move on.

pitfalls: One vector for 'bank' — polysemy needs context.
Ignoring subword — FastText for morphologically rich text.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Train FastText on a small corpus; inspect nearest neighbors.

lessons.title: One Vector for 'bank': The Polysemy Problem
concepts: Static embeddings conflate meanings — 'bank' (river) vs 'bank' (money) share one vector.
Contextual embeddings (ELMo, BERT) produce per-occurrence vectors — polysemy solved.
This motivated the transformer era: meaning depends on context.
Lesson: representation must match the task's ambiguity.

example.code:
POLYSEMY:
  Static: bank → [0.2, -0.5, ...] (one)
  Contextual: bank|river → v1, bank|money → v2
example.walkthrough: If your task has ambiguity, you need contextual representations.

pitfalls: Static for WSD — wrong tool.
Ignoring the cost — contextual needs more compute.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Find 5 polysemous words; show static vs contextual handling.

lessons.title: Sentence Embeddings
concepts: Sentence transformers: siamese/triplet training for semantic similarity — the retrieval workhorse.
Pooling: mean of token vectors (with attention mask) — simple, effective.
Multilingual variants (paraphrase-multilingual) cover 50+ languages.
Use for: semantic search, clustering, deduplication, RAG retrieval.

example.code:
SENTENCE EMBEDDING USE:
  search, cluster, dedupe, rerank
  → all need sentence-level similarity
example.walkthrough: This is the embedding you will actually deploy most.

pitfalls: Averaging without masks — padding pollutes.
Wrong domain — fine-tune on your data.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Build a semantic search over 1000 docs; eval 20 queries.

lessons.title: Fine-Tuning Embeddings
concepts: Domain shift hurts: fine-tune embedding models on your corpus with contrastive loss.
Hard negatives matter most — mine them (e.g., top-k wrong retrievals).
Evaluate on YOUR retrieval task, not generic benchmarks.
Small data? Start with adapters or just the top layers.

example.code:
FINE-TUNE LOOP:
  Mine hard negatives → contrastive train
  → eval recall@k on domain queries → repeat
example.walkthrough: Hard negatives are the secret ingredient.

pitfalls: Random negatives only — too easy, no learning.
Generic benchmarks — measure your task.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Mine hard negatives for 50 queries; fine-tune; measure delta.

lessons.title: Vector Databases
concepts: Store + ANN search: FAISS, Qdrant, Pinecone, pgvector — pick by scale and ops.
HNSW: fast recall, memory-hungry. IVF: balanced. Match to your constraints.
Metadata filtering + hybrid (dense + BM25) — production retrieval patterns.
Monitor: recall, latency p99, index freshness.

example.code:
VECTOR DB CHOICE:
  Prototype → FAISS/pgvector
  Production → Qdrant/Pinecone (managed)
  Always: metadata + hybrid
example.walkthrough: The DB is infrastructure — evaluate ops burden too.

pitfalls: No metadata — unfilterable.
Stale index — freshness pipeline needed.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Index 10k docs in FAISS; benchmark recall and p99 latency.

lessons.title: RNNs: Sequences with Memory
concepts: RNN: hidden state carries history — h_t = f(h_{t-1}, x_t).
Vanishing gradients: long dependencies fade — the fundamental RNN limit.
Where they still win: tiny models, streaming, strict latency budgets.
Understand RNNs to appreciate why transformers took over.

example.code:
RNN CORE:
  h_t = tanh(W_h·h_{t-1} + W_x·x_t)
  Output from h_t; state = memory
example.walkthrough: Implement a char-RNN — the intuition is worth the hour.

pitfalls: Long docs with vanilla RNN — gradients vanish.
Ignoring the lesson — know WHY transformers won.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Train a char-RNN on tiny Shakespeare; sample text.

lessons.title: LSTMs and GRUs: Gated Memory
concepts: Gates (input/forget/output) control information flow — LSTMs remember longer.
GRU: simplified (reset/update gates) — fewer params, similar performance.
Still relevant: on-device, low-latency, small-data sequence tasks.
Bidirectional LSTMs: past + future context for tagging tasks.

example.code:
LSTM GATES:
  forget: what to drop | input: what to add
  output: what to emit
  Cell state = the conveyor belt
example.walkthrough: Gates are the innovation — understand each one's job.

pitfalls: Vanilla RNN for long sequences — use gated.
Unidirectional for tagging — bidirectional helps.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Compare RNN vs LSTM on a 50-step dependency task.

lessons.title: When NOT to Use Transformers
concepts: Tiny data: LSTMs/CRFs with features beat data-hungry transformers.
Strict latency: distilled LSTMs run in microseconds on CPU.
Streaming: RNNs are naturally online; transformers need caching tricks.
Engineering rule: simplest model that meets the bar.

example.code:
MODEL LADDER:
  Baseline: logistic regression / LSTM
  Then: small transformer
  Only then: large transformer
example.walkthrough: Climb the ladder — don't start at the top.

pitfalls: Transformer default-ism — measure the simpler baseline.
Ignoring latency budgets — they decide.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Benchmark LSTM vs tiny transformer on your task (acc + latency).

lessons.title: CRFs for Structured Prediction
concepts: CRF: models label DEPENDENCIES (BIO tags can't be invalid) — NER/POS classic.
BiLSTM-CRF was the NER standard before transformers.
Still useful: constrained decoding, low-resource tagging.
Modern use: CRF layer atop transformer encoders.

example.code:
CRF VALUE:
  Learns: 'I-ORG can't follow B-PER'
  Global sequence optimum, not greedy
example.walkthrough: Label dependencies are real constraints — model them.

pitfalls: Independent softmax per token — invalid sequences.
CRF everywhere — transformers often suffice.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Add a CRF head to a tagger; measure invalid-sequence rate.

lessons.title: From Sequences to Attention
concepts: History: RNN → LSTM → attention → transformer — each solved the last's bottleneck.
Attention solved long dependencies; transformers parallelized training.
What survived: gating ideas, bidirectionality, sequence losses.
Knowing the lineage makes modern architectures legible.

example.code:
LINEAGE:
  RNN (memory) → LSTM (gates) →
  Attention (access) → Transformer (parallel)
example.walkthrough: Each step is a response to a bottleneck — learn the pattern.

pitfalls: History as trivia — it explains design choices.
Ignoring survivors — old ideas recur.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Write the 4-step lineage with each step's bottleneck+solution.

lessons.title: HuggingFace Ecosystem
concepts: Transformers library: models, tokenizers, pipelines — the standard toolkit.
Hub: 500k+ models and datasets — start from pretrained, don't train from scratch.
Datasets + Evaluate + Accelerate: data, metrics, and distributed training helpers.
Pipelines for prototyping; custom code for production.

example.code:
HF WORKFLOW:
  pipeline() → prototype
  AutoModel → customize
  Trainer → fine-tune
  Hub → share
example.walkthrough: The Hub is leverage — use it.

pitfalls: Training from scratch — wasteful 99% of the time.
Pipeline in production — inflexible.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Fine-tune a Hub model on a small dataset today.

lessons.title: Fine-Tuning in Practice
concepts: Full vs LoRA/QLoRA: parameter-efficient is the default — 1% of weights, 95% of gains.
Hyperparams: LR 1e-5–5e-5, few epochs, warmup — small and careful.
Watch for: catastrophic forgetting, overfitting small data, eval leakage.
Evaluate on YOUR task — GLUE scores don't transfer.

example.code:
FINETUNE RECIPE:
  LoRA r=16, all linear | LR 2e-5
  3 epochs | eval every 500 steps
  Best checkpoint by YOUR metric
example.walkthrough: Small LR, few epochs, your eval — the mantra.

pitfalls: High LR — destroys pretrained knowledge.
No held-out eval — flying blind.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: LoRA-tune a classifier; plot train vs eval loss.

lessons.title: Debugging Training
concepts: Loss not decreasing: LR too low/high, data bug, or frozen backbone mistake.
Loss NaN: LR too high, mixed precision overflow — clip, scale, bf16.
Overfitting: more data, augmentation, dropout, early stopping.
Instrument: W&B/TensorBoard from run one — no blind training.

example.code:
DEBUG LADDER:
  Data batch → forward shapes → loss value
  → gradients flow? → LR sane? → overfit small subset?
example.walkthrough: Overfit a tiny subset first — if it can't, something's broken.

pitfalls: Blind training — log everything.
Skipping the tiny-subset test.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Deliberately break a training run; diagnose using the ladder.

lessons.title: Inference Optimization Basics
concepts: Batching: throughput vs latency — tune per SLO.
Quantization: int8/fp8 for serving — measure accuracy delta.
Distillation: small student for latency-critical paths.
Profile first: find the bottleneck (compute vs memory-bound) before optimizing.

example.code:
OPTIMIZE ORDER:
  Profile → batch → quantize → distill
  Measure each step's delta
example.walkthrough: Optimization without profiling is guessing.

pitfalls: Premature optimization — profile first.
Accuracy-blind quantization.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Profile inference: where does time go?

lessons.title: Reproducibility
concepts: Seeds: Python, NumPy, PyTorch, CUDA — set all, log all.
Versions: pin transformers, torch, CUDA — environments drift.
Data: version datasets (DVC/HF datasets revisions).
One-command repro: README + script + env file = rerunnable.

example.code:
REPRO KIT:
  requirements.txt | seeds logged
  data version | run script | README
example.walkthrough: If a colleague can't rerun it, it's not done.

pitfalls: Unpinned envs — 'worked on my machine'.
Unversioned data — silent drift.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Package your last experiment as a repro kit.

lessons.title: Pipeline Anatomy
concepts: Stages: ingest → preprocess → model → postprocess → store/serve — each independently testable.
Contracts between stages: schemas, not vibes — validate at boundaries.
Idempotency: re-running a stage is safe — design for retries.

steps: Create lab1.py: download the NLTK 'punkt', 'averaged_perceptron_tagger', 'maxent_ne_chunker', and 'words' resources, then load three short news-style paragraphs as your corpus.
For each paragraph, run sentence segmentation, word tokenization, POS tagging, and nltk.ne_chunk; print the tagged sentences and extracted entity trees.
Collect all PERSON/ORGANIZATION/GPE entities into a list and print the unique set with counts.
Hand-annotate the true entities for one paragraph (your gold standard) and compute precision/recall of the chunker against it.
In three sentences, state where the classical pipeline is trustworthy, where it fails, and which failure mode a neural NER model would fix first.

checks.hint: Print the extracted entity labels (e.g. lines containing PERSON/ORGANIZATION/GPE) so the check can see the chunker ran.

labs.title: Fine-tune a text classifier end to end
labs.objective: Fine-tune a small transformer classifier on a labeled text dataset with the Trainer API, using proper fine-tuning discipline, and report validation metrics plus a model-card-style summary.
steps: Create lab2.py: build a tiny labeled CSV (at least 200 rows, 2-3 classes, e.g. support-ticket topics) and load it with the datasets library.

Tokenize with the matching AutoTokenizer (distilbert-base-uncased), create AutoModelForSequenceClassification with num_labels set, and configure TrainingArguments: lr=2e-5, 3 epochs, evaluation each epoch.
Train with Trainer, then evaluate on a held-out split and print accuracy and macro F1 to four decimals.
Run the base pipeline (no fine-tuning) on the same held-out split and print its accuracy — the baseline your fine-tune had to beat.
Write a five-line model card: base checkpoint, training data description, eval metrics, known limits, intended use.

checks.hint: Print a line like 'macro F1 0.XXXX' after evaluation so the check can see the metric.

simulations.title: Search returns junk after reindex
simulations.brief: The semantic search index was rebuilt last night. Since then, relevant documents rank below random ones and recall collapsed.

steps.symptom: Recall collapsed after a routine reindex; no code changes.
evidence: Reindex used embedding model v3; the previous index was built with v2
The same document embeds to a different vector under v3 — the vector space changed
Queries are still embedded with v2 at request time
options: Rebuild the index with the pinned v2 model and lock the embedding model version in the index config
Retrain the ranking model on the new v3 vectors
Increase ef_search to compensate for the worse recall
Delete the index and rebuild it the same way — reindexes are flaky
steps.explain: Documents embedded with v3 live in a different vector space than queries embedded with v2 — cosine similarity across spaces is meaningless. The embedding model is part of the index contract: pin it, version it, and rebuild the index whenever it changes.

simulations.debrief: An embedding index is a contract between the indexed vectors and the query vectors. Change the embedding model and the contract breaks — pin the model version and rebuild on every change.

simulations.title: p99 latency spike
simulations.brief: The embedding service p99 latency tripled after traffic doubled. p50 barely moved — the tail is the problem.

steps.symptom: p99 latency 3x, p50 flat, after a traffic doubling.
evidence: One document per inference request — no batching
Kernel launches dominate; the GPU idles between tiny requests
Requests pile up behind each other at peak; p50 requests slip through the gaps
options: Add dynamic batching so concurrent requests share GPU kernel launches
Add more GPUs to handle the doubled traffic
Cache embeddings for the most common documents
Reduce the embedding dimension to speed up each request
steps.explain: Unbatched single-doc inference wastes the GPU on kernel-launch overhead; doubling traffic turned the queue into a tail-latency disaster. Dynamic batching amortizes the launch cost across concurrent requests — p99 drops without new hardware.

simulations.debrief: Tail latency in embedding services is usually a batching problem, not a hardware problem. Batch concurrent requests dynamically before buying GPUs.

simulations.title: Pick the chunking strategy
simulations.brief: You are indexing 10,000-page technical manuals for retrieval. Choose the chunking strategy.

choices.label: Overlapping fixed-size chunks with section metadata (page, heading, doc id)
choices.feedback: Correct: overlap preserves context across boundaries, and metadata lets the system cite and filter precisely. Retrieval needs addressable, self-contained chunks.

choices.label: One chunk per whole document — the model can handle long context
choices.feedback: Whole-document chunks dilute the embedding: one vector cannot represent 500 pages, and retrieval precision collapses. Long context is not a chunking strategy.

simulations.debrief: Chunk for retrieval, not for reading: overlapping, metadata-rich, self-contained passages. The embedding represents the chunk — make each chunk represent one thing.

simulations.title: Build the search pipeline
simulations.brief: Put the semantic search pipeline steps in build order.

steps.context: A sound search pipeline build order
items: Embed the chunks with the pinned model
Chunk the documents with overlap and metadata
Rerank the top candidates with a cross-encoder
Retrieve top-k candidates from the vector index
Build the vector index over the embeddings

simulations.debrief: Chunk first (retrieval quality starts here), embed with the pinned model, index, retrieve broadly, then rerank narrowly. Reranking before retrieval is wasted compute; indexing before chunking is impossible.

simulations.title: Review the index config
simulations.brief: This vector index config is headed to production. Click the misconfigured lines (2 issues to find).

steps.config:
index: hnsw
 dim: 768
embedding_model: null
metric: cosine
ef_search: 16
rebuild_on_model_change: false

issues.description: No embedding model pinned — the next model swap silently breaks the query/index contract.
issues.fix: Pin the embedding model name and version (e.g. emb-v2).

issues.description: No rebuild on model change — a future embedding update leaves a stale, mismatched index in production.
issues.fix: Set rebuild_on_model_change to true so the index rebuilds with the new model.

simulations.debrief: Index configs must encode the embedding contract: pinned model version and automatic rebuilds on change. A config that allows silent drift is a future outage.

sections.title: Natural Language Processing Engineering — core path

behavioral.prompt: Explain word embeddings to a product manager who thinks the model 'understands English like a person does.'
points: Give the distributional intuition in one plain sentence
Name one concrete limit (polysemy, bias, no grounding) with an example
Connect the limit to a product decision they own
Check their understanding with a question, not a lecture
pitfalls: Letting the anthropomorphism stand
Drowning them in vector math
No product implication drawn

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time your NLP model produced biased or harmful output. What did you do?
points: Describe the output and how it was caught
Trace it to data, representation, or decoding — with evidence
Explain the mitigation and how you measured it
State what monitoring you added afterward
pitfalls: Denying the model can be biased
Blaming the training data and stopping there
No measurement of the fix

behavioral.prompt: Walk me through shipping a text feature built on messy, real-world user input.
points: Characterize the mess: languages, noise, length, edge cases
Explain the preprocessing and tokenization choices and why
Describe how you evaluated on realistic data, not clean benchmarks
Name what broke in production and how you handled it
pitfalls: Assuming clean input
Evaluating only on a tidy benchmark
No error analysis on real failures

behavioral.prompt: Describe a disagreement about whether to use a classical NLP approach or a neural model.
points: State the task constraints both sides faced (latency, data, interpretability)
Show the baseline comparison that informed the call
Explain the final decision and its measured tradeoff
Note what would flip the decision
pitfalls: Choosing neural by default prestige
No baseline numbers
Ignoring latency or cost constraints

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a labeling or annotation effort you ran or relied on. How did you ensure quality?
points: Describe the guidelines and how annotators were trained
Explain how you measured agreement
Show how label noise affected the model, with numbers
Describe the adjudication process for disagreements
pitfalls: Treating labels as ground truth without checking
No agreement measurement
Blaming the model for label noise

behavioral.prompt: How do you evaluate a language model beyond a single accuracy number?
points: Name the metric suite for the task (precision/recall/F1, BLEU/ROUGE limits, human eval)
Explain slicing: performance by subgroup, length, or domain
Describe error analysis on real failures
Connect metrics to the user-facing outcome
pitfalls: One metric to rule them all
No error analysis
Metrics disconnected from user impact

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you had to read a model card or paper critically before using a checkpoint.
points: Name what you checked: training data, domain, license, limits
Describe a red flag you found and how it changed your plan
Explain how you validated the checkpoint on your data
State the usage constraints you documented
pitfalls: Downloading the top-of-leaderboard checkpoint blindly
Ignoring the license
No validation on own data

behavioral.prompt: Describe a production incident involving an NLP system — drift, bad outputs, or a pipeline failure.
points: Explain how the failure surfaced and its user impact
Trace the root cause (data drift, domain shift, tokenizer mismatch)
Describe the fix and the guardrail added
State what you monitor now that you did not before
pitfalls: Blaming users for weird input
A fix with no monitoring
No root-cause chain

cheatsheet: Preprocessing serves the task: keep negations for sentiment; normalize aggressively only for retrieval-style tasks.
Subword tokenizers (BPE/WordPiece) for noisy or open-vocabulary text; word-level only for clean, closed domains.
Static embeddings (Word2Vec/GloVe): one vector per word type. Contextual: one per occurrence.
pipeline() first for baselines; read the model card before trusting any checkpoint.
Fine-tune gently: lr ~2e-5, few epochs, warmup, early stopping on validation.
Decoding shapes output: greedy is myopic; beam/sampling + repetition penalty for open-ended generation.
NLTK classics are baselines and features: fast, inspectable, still winning small well-defined tasks.
Evaluate on your data and your task — never on the checkpoint's home benchmark alone.
glossary: tokenization
Splitting text into the units a model consumes: words, subwords, or characters.
BPE / WordPiece
Subword tokenization algorithms that merge frequent character pairs; handle rare words via known pieces.
OOV
Out-of-vocabulary: tokens unseen in training; word-level models map them all to one UNK vector.
Word2Vec / GloVe
Static word-embedding methods from the distributional hypothesis: one vector per word type.
contextual embedding
A token vector computed from its surrounding context (e.g. BERT); disambiguates word senses.
POS tagging
Labeling each token with its part of speech (noun, verb, ...); a classical sequence-labeling task.
NER
Named entity recognition: finding and typing spans like PERSON, ORGANIZATION, GPE.
chunking / parsing
Grouping tokens into phrases (chunking) or full syntactic trees (parsing).
RNN / LSTM
Recurrent architectures carrying hidden state across tokens; LSTMs add gates for long-range memory.
seq2seq
Encoder-decoder architecture mapping an input sequence to an output sequence (translation, summarization).
attention
Mechanism letting the decoder weight encoder states per output step; the original seq2seq attention predates transformers.
decoding
Strategy for choosing output tokens: greedy, beam search, or sampling (temperature, top-k, top-p).
language modeling
Predicting the next token given context; the unifying pretraining task for modern NLP.
fine-tuning
Continuing training of a pretrained model on task data with a small learning rate.
model card
Documentation for a checkpoint: training data, intended use, limits, license — read before downloading.
domain shift
When deployment text differs from training text; degrades performance and calibration.
pipeline (HF)
Hugging Face's high-level API: tokenizer + model + postprocessing in one call.
Trainer
Hugging Face's training loop abstraction handling batching, optimization, and evaluation.

links.label: AirLLM
links.note: Run 70B+ parameter models on a 4GB GPU via layer-wise inference — streams one layer at a time through VRAM, no quantization or pruning required. Open-source; supports Llama, Qwen, Mistral.

checklist: Preprocessing choices justified per task; negations preserved where meaning depends on them.
Tokenizer matched to text noise level; OOV rate measured on real data.
Baseline established (classical or pipeline) before any fine-tuning.
Model card read: training domain, license, and known limits documented.
Fine-tuning uses low LR, few epochs, warmup, and validation-based early stopping.
Evaluation on in-domain held-out data with task-appropriate metrics and error analysis.
Decoding strategy chosen deliberately for generation tasks.
Known failure modes (domain shift, polysemy, label noise) listed with mitigations.
